questions.enonce_markdown:
Examine Leibniz's contributions to theology and theodicy.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646-1716), a German philosopher, mathematician and diplomat, made important contributions to the philosophy of religion. He coined the word "theodicy" (from the Greek *theos*, God, and *dike*, justice) as the title of his book *Theodicy* (1710), written to defend God's goodness and justice in the face of evil.

**1. Contributions to theology.**
- *Arguments for the existence of God.* Leibniz developed the cosmological argument from contingency. Nothing exists without a sufficient reason (the principle of sufficient reason). The world is a collection of contingent things, and so its sufficient reason must lie outside it, in a necessary being, God. He also refined the ontological argument by arguing that one must show that the idea of a perfect being is possible, that is, free of contradiction, and if it is possible a perfect being must exist.
- *Pre-established harmony.* He taught that created substances (monads) do not act on each other but are arranged by God so that they harmonise perfectly. God is the guarantor of the order of the universe.
- *Rational religion.* Leibniz held that faith and reason do not contradict each other; revelation may go beyond reason but not against it.
- *Concern for Christian unity.* He took part in efforts to reconcile the Protestant and Catholic churches.

**2. Theodicy: the problem.** If God is all-powerful, all-knowing and all-good, why is there evil? Leibniz distinguished three types: *metaphysical evil* (the limitation or imperfection of all created things), *physical evil* (pain and suffering) and *moral evil* (sin).

**3. Leibniz's answer.**
- *The best of all possible worlds.* Among infinite possible worlds, God, in his wisdom and goodness, chose to create the best one. A better world was not possible, even though it contains evil, because the best world is the one with the greatest overall perfection and variety, and its parts are interconnected, so removing an evil might spoil the whole.
- *Evil is permitted, not willed.* God does not will evil as an end, but permits it as a condition of the greater good. Moral evil results from human free will; God foresaw it but did not cause it.
- *Evil as lack.* Following Augustine, he treats evil as a privation of good.
- *Suffering may serve good ends,* such as the improvement of character, and the world is seen as a whole.

**4. Evaluation.**
- *Strengths:* his answer protects God's omnipotence and goodness and takes human freedom seriously. It has influenced later free-will defences and "soul-making" approaches.
- *Criticisms:* Voltaire mocked the optimism in *Candide* after the Lisbon earthquake (1755). If this is the best world, then why strive to improve it? It is hard to accept that the suffering of innocents, such as children, is justified by a greater whole. Many questions about whether God could have created free beings without evil remain. Hume and Kant also challenged the possibility of arriving at such knowledge by reason alone.

**Conclusion.** Leibniz contributed arguments for God's existence and, above all, the first systematic theodicy. His claim that this is the best of all possible worlds is bold and influential, but remains controversial in face of the extent of suffering.
